claim: Multiple alphaviruses, including chikungunya (CHIKV), Ross River (RRV), and o'nyong 'nyong (ONNV) viruses, are cleared from the circulation of mice by liver Kupffer cells.
source: We find that multiple alphaviruses, including chikungunya (CHIKV), Ross River (RRV), and o'nyong 'nyong (ONNV) viruses, are cleared from the circulation of mice by liver Kupffer cells, impeding viral dissemination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing viral clearance in mice treated with clodronate liposomes and viral accumulation in liver tissue (Figures 1, 2).

claim: Clearance of alphaviruses from the circulation is independent of natural antibodies.
source: Clearance from the circulation was independent of natural antibodies or complement factor C3, and instead relied on scavenger receptor SR-A6 (MARCO).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in B cell deficient μMT mice showing efficient viral clearance (Figure 3B).

claim: Clearance of alphaviruses from the circulation is independent of complement factor C3.
source: Clearance from the circulation was independent of natural antibodies or complement factor C3, and instead relied on scavenger receptor SR-A6 (MARCO).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in C3-/- mice showing efficient viral clearance (Figure 3A).

claim: Clearance of alphaviruses from the circulation relies on scavenger receptor SR-A6 (MARCO).
source: Clearance from the circulation was independent of natural antibodies or complement factor C3, and instead relied on scavenger receptor SR-A6 (MARCO).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing impaired viral clearance in MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3F, G, H).

claim: Lysine to arginine substitutions at E2 K200 in CHIKV and ONNV allow for escape from clearance.
source: Remarkably, lysine to arginine substitutions at distinct residues within the E2 glycoproteins of CHIKV and ONNV (E2 K200R) as well as RRV (E2 K251R) allowed for escape from clearance and enhanced viremia and dissemination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing CHIKV E2 K200R and ONNV E2 K200R particles remain in circulation (Figures 4, 5).

claim: Lysine to arginine substitution at E2 K251 in RRV allows for escape from clearance.
source: Remarkably, lysine to arginine substitutions at distinct residues within the E2 glycoproteins of CHIKV and ONNV (E2 K200R) as well as RRV (E2 K251R) allowed for escape from clearance and enhanced viremia and dissemination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing RRV E2 K251R particles remain in circulation (Figure 7).

claim: Viral clearance from the circulation is strictly dependent on the presence of lysine at E2 200 (CHIKV) or E2 251 (RRV).
source: Mutational analysis revealed that viral clearance from the circulation is strictly dependent on the presence of lysine at these positions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing all amino acid substitutions away from lysine at these positions allow clearance evasion (Figure 8).

claim: DENVs are estimated to cause ~390 million infections per year.
source: For example, DENVs are estimated to cause ~390 million infections per year resulting in ~500,000 cases of dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome that can result in death (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: DENVs result in ~500,000 cases of dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome.
source: For example, DENVs are estimated to cause ~390 million infections per year resulting in ~500,000 cases of dengue hemorrhagic fever/dengue shock syndrome that can result in death (Bhatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhatt et al., 2013.

claim: Since 2004, CHIKV has infected millions of people and expanded into Europe, Asia, the Pacific region, and the Americas.
source: Since 2004, CHIKV has infected millions of people and expanded into Europe, Asia, the Pacific region, and the Americas (Moro et al., 2010; Volk et al., 2010; Zeller et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moro et al., 2010; Volk et al., 2010; Zeller et al., 2016.

claim: Joint pain, swelling, and stiffness, and tenosynovitis, can endure for months to years after CHIKV infection.
source: Joint pain, swelling, and stiffness, and tenosynovitis, can endure for months to years after CHIKV infection (Borgherini et al., 2008; Couturier et al., 2012; Gérardin et al., 2011; Rodriguez-Morales et al., 2016; Schilte et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Borgherini et al., 2008; Couturier et al., 2012; Gérardin et al., 2011; Rodriguez-Morales et al., 2016; Schilte et al., 2013.

claim: Large CHIKV epidemics have severe economic impact.
source: As chronic CHIKV disease is debilitating, large epidemics have severe economic impact (Cardona-Ospina et al., 2015; Soumahoro et al., 2011; Vijayakumar et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cardona-Ospina et al., 2015; Soumahoro et al., 2011; Vijayakumar et al., 2013.

claim: ZIKV caused outbreaks on Yap Island in 2007.
source: ZIKV caused outbreaks on Yap Island (Duffy et al., 2009) and islands of French Polynesia (Musso et al., 2018) in 2007 and 2013, respectively, before being introduced to the Americas (Metsky et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: ZIKV caused outbreaks on islands of French Polynesia in 2013.
source: ZIKV caused outbreaks on Yap Island (Duffy et al., 2009) and islands of French Polynesia (Musso et al., 2018) in 2007 and 2013, respectively, before being introduced to the Americas (Metsky et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Musso et al., 2018.

claim: ZIKV was introduced to the Americas after outbreaks in the Pacific.
source: ZIKV caused outbreaks on Yap Island (Duffy et al., 2009) and islands of French Polynesia (Musso et al., 2018) in 2007 and 2013, respectively, before being introduced to the Americas (Metsky et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Metsky et al., 2017.

claim: ZIKV caused nearly one million confirmed and suspected cases in the Americas.
source: Here, ZIKV caused nearly one million confirmed and suspected cases and became recognized as a cause of congenital neurodevelopmental defects (Pierson and Diamond, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierson and Diamond, 2018.

claim: ZIKV is recognized as a cause of congenital neurodevelopmental defects.
source: Here, ZIKV caused nearly one million confirmed and suspected cases and became recognized as a cause of congenital neurodevelopmental defects (Pierson and Diamond, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pierson and Diamond, 2018.

claim: The magnitude and duration of viremia in vertebrate hosts are important determinants of arboviral emergence, transmission efficiency, and geographic spread.
source: The magnitude and duration of viremia in vertebrate hosts are important determinants of arboviral emergence, transmission efficiency, and geographic spread (Weaver, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weaver, 2018.

claim: For many arboviruses, viremia levels correlate with disease severity.
source: Moreover, for many arboviruses, viremia levels correlate with disease severity (Chow et al., 2011; de St Maurice et al., 2018; Pozo-Aguilar et al., 2014; Vaughn et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chow et al., 2011; de St Maurice et al., 2018; Pozo-Aguilar et al., 2014; Vaughn et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2016.

claim: In PLL-treated mice, CHIKV and RRV viral particles were nearly undetectable in the serum by 45 min post-inoculation.
source: In PLL-treated mice, viral particles (CHIKV and RRV) or plaque forming units (ONNV) were nearly undetectable in the serum by 45 min post-inoculation (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In PLL-treated mice, ONNV plaque forming units were nearly undetectable in the serum by 45 min post-inoculation.
source: In PLL-treated mice, viral particles (CHIKV and RRV) or plaque forming units (ONNV) were nearly undetectable in the serum by 45 min post-inoculation (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CLL-treated mice had 3–4 orders of magnitude higher amounts of CHIKV and RRV viral particles in the serum at 45 min post-inoculation compared to PLL-treated mice.
source: In stark contrast, CLL-treated mice had 3–4 orders of magnitude higher amounts of viral particles (CHIKV and RRV) or plaque-forming units (ONNV) in the serum at this time point (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CLL-treated mice had 3–4 orders of magnitude higher amounts of ONNV plaque-forming units in the serum at 45 min post-inoculation compared to PLL-treated mice.
source: In stark contrast, CLL-treated mice had 3–4 orders of magnitude higher amounts of viral particles (CHIKV and RRV) or plaque-forming units (ONNV) in the serum at this time point (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CHIKV was efficiently cleared from the circulation of splenectomized mice.
source: CHIKV was efficiently cleared from the circulation of splenectomized mice (Figure 2A), demonstrating that the spleen is not required for clearance of circulating CHIKV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The spleen is not required for clearance of circulating CHIKV.
source: CHIKV was efficiently cleared from the circulation of splenectomized mice (Figure 2A), demonstrating that the spleen is not required for clearance of circulating CHIKV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in splenectomized mice shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CLL-pretreatment blocked CHIKV clearance in splenectomized mice.
source: Moreover, CLL-pretreatment blocked CHIKV clearance in splenectomized mice (Figure 2B), suggesting that the remaining phagocytic cells in the liver are sufficient to clear CHIKV from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Phagocytic cells in the liver are sufficient to clear CHIKV from the circulation.
source: Moreover, CLL-pretreatment blocked CHIKV clearance in splenectomized mice (Figure 2B), suggesting that the remaining phagocytic cells in the liver are sufficient to clear CHIKV from the circulation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing clearance in splenectomized mice that is blocked by CLL treatment (Figure 2B).

claim: CHIKV RNA accumulated in the liver of control PLL-treated mice.
source: Consistent with this, CHIKV RNA accumulated in the liver of control PLL-treated mice, and this specific accumulation was lost in CLL-treated mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CHIKV RNA accumulation in the liver was lost in CLL-treated mice.
source: Consistent with this, CHIKV RNA accumulated in the liver of control PLL-treated mice, and this specific accumulation was lost in CLL-treated mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Viral RNA levels increased in the spleen and lung of CLL-treated mice compared with control PLL-treated mice.
source: In contrast, viral RNA levels increased in the spleen and lung of CLL-treated mice compared with control PLL-treated mice (Figure 2C), likely due to the high amounts of virus present in contaminating blood.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CHIKV RNA is readily detectable by in situ hybridization in the livers of PLL-treated mice at 45 min post-inoculation.
source: Moreover, CHIKV RNA is readily detectable by in situ hybridization in the livers of PLL-treated mice at 45 min post-inoculation, but not in CLL-treated mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CHIKV RNA is not detectable by in situ hybridization in the livers of CLL-treated mice at 45 min post-inoculation.
source: Moreover, CHIKV RNA is readily detectable by in situ hybridization in the livers of PLL-treated mice at 45 min post-inoculation, but not in CLL-treated mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment of mice with CLL resulted in depletion of F4/80+ liver macrophages.
source: While both dendritic cells (DCs) and macrophages can sequester pathogens in the liver (Jenne and Kubes, 2013), treatment of mice with CLL resulted in depletion of F4/80+ liver macrophages (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2) but had minimal impact on CD11c+ DCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting macrophages are responsible for alphavirus clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CLL treatment had minimal impact on CD11c+ DCs in the liver.
source: While both dendritic cells (DCs) and macrophages can sequester pathogens in the liver (Jenne and Kubes, 2013), treatment of mice with CLL resulted in depletion of F4/80+ liver macrophages (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2) but had minimal impact on CD11c+ DCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting macrophages are responsible for alphavirus clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Macrophages are responsible for alphavirus clearance.
source: While both dendritic cells (DCs) and macrophages can sequester pathogens in the liver (Jenne and Kubes, 2013), treatment of mice with CLL resulted in depletion of F4/80+ liver macrophages (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2) but had minimal impact on CD11c+ DCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting macrophages are responsible for alphavirus clearance.
evidence: Inferred from selective depletion of macrophages but not DCs by CLL treatment and loss of viral clearance (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: CHIKV and RRV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of C3-/- mice.
source: However, CHIKV and RRV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of C3-/- (Figure 3A) and B cell deficient μMT mice (Figure 3B), which lack C3 and circulating IgM and IgG, respectively (Kitamura et al., 1991; Wessels et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CHIKV and RRV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of B cell deficient μMT mice.
source: However, CHIKV and RRV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of C3-/- (Figure 3A) and B cell deficient μMT mice (Figure 3B), which lack C3 and circulating IgM and IgG, respectively (Kitamura et al., 1991; Wessels et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Clearance of circulating alphavirus particles is independent of receptors for fragments of C3 and of Fc receptors.
source: These data suggest that clearance of circulating alphavirus particles is independent of receptors for fragments of C3 and of Fc receptors.
evidence: Inferred from efficient clearance in C3-/- and μMT mice (Figure 3A, B).

claim: Poly(I) pretreatment potently inhibited the clearance of circulating CHIKV and RRV particles.
source: Similar to pretreatment with CLL, poly(I) pretreatment potently inhibited the clearance of circulating CHIKV and RRV particles (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pretreatment of mice with dextran sulfate inhibited clearance of circulating CHIKV and RRV particles.
source: Similar results were observed following pretreatment of mice with dextran sulfate (DS), another SR ligand (Platt and Gordon, 1998) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SR-A1 (MSR1), SR-A6 (MARCO), SR-B1 (SCARB1), SR-B2 (CD36), and SR-I1 (CD163) mRNAs are robustly expressed in Kupffer cells.
source: To identify SRs that are expressed by KCs, we mined publicly available single-cell transcriptomic data of the mouse liver (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018), and found SR-A1 (MSR1), SR-A6 (MARCO), SR-B1 (SCARB1), SR-B2 (CD36), and SR-I1 (CD163) mRNAs to be robustly expressed in KCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SR-A1 and MARCO bind poly(I) and dextran sulfate.
source: Of these, only SR-A1 and MARCO are known to bind poly(I) and DS (Chen et al., 2006; Platt and Gordon, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2006; Platt and Gordon, 1998.

claim: CHIKV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of SR-A1-/- mice.
source: CHIKV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of SR-A1-/- mice, and this clearance was inhibited by pre-treatment of SR-A1-/- mice with poly(I) (Figure 3E), indicating that CHIKV clearance was still occurring through a SR-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CHIKV clearance in SR-A1-/- mice was inhibited by pre-treatment with poly(I).
source: CHIKV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of SR-A1-/- mice, and this clearance was inhibited by pre-treatment of SR-A1-/- mice with poly(I) (Figure 3E), indicating that CHIKV clearance was still occurring through a SR-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CHIKV clearance in SR-A1-/- mice occurs through a SR-dependent mechanism.
source: CHIKV particles were efficiently cleared from the circulation of SR-A1-/- mice, and this clearance was inhibited by pre-treatment of SR-A1-/- mice with poly(I) (Figure 3E), indicating that CHIKV clearance was still occurring through a SR-dependent mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from inhibition of clearance by poly(I) in SR-A1-/- mice (Figure 3E).

claim: CHIKV particles remained readily detectable in the serum of MARCO-/- mice at 45 min post-inoculation.
source: In contrast, CHIKV particles remained readily detectable in the serum of MARCO-/- mice at 45 min post-inoculation (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Pretreatment with CLL blocked clearance of circulating CHIKV particles in WT mice but had no effect in MARCO-/- mice.
source: Moreover, whereas pretreatment with CLL blocked clearance of circulating CHIKV particles in WT mice, this treatment had no effect on the level of CHIKV in the circulation of MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: CHIKV RNA was detectable by in situ hybridization in the liver of PLL-treated WT mice.
source: Furthermore, CHIKV RNA was detectable by in situ hybridization in the liver of PLL-treated WT mice, but not in the liver of PLL-treated MARCO-/- mice or CLL-treated WT and MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: CHIKV RNA was not detectable by in situ hybridization in the liver of PLL-treated MARCO-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, CHIKV RNA was detectable by in situ hybridization in the liver of PLL-treated WT mice, but not in the liver of PLL-treated MARCO-/- mice or CLL-treated WT and MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: CHIKV RNA was not detectable by in situ hybridization in the liver of CLL-treated WT and MARCO-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, CHIKV RNA was detectable by in situ hybridization in the liver of PLL-treated WT mice, but not in the liver of PLL-treated MARCO-/- mice or CLL-treated WT and MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: WT and MARCO-/- mice had a similar number of KCs in the liver.
source: Despite the virological differences in the circulation and liver of PLL-treated WT and MARCO-/- mice, these mice had a similar number of KCs in the liver (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Both WT and MARCO-/- KCs were efficiently depleted by CLL.
source: Finally, both WT and MARCO-/- KCs were efficiently depleted by CLL (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that MARCO-/- KCs retain phagocytic capacity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: MARCO-/- KCs retain phagocytic capacity.
source: Finally, both WT and MARCO-/- KCs were efficiently depleted by CLL (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that MARCO-/- KCs retain phagocytic capacity.
evidence: Inferred from efficient depletion of MARCO-/- KCs by CLL (Figure 3H and I).

claim: MARCO is essential for clearance of CHIKV particles from the circulation.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that MARCO is essential for clearance of CHIKV particles from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing impaired clearance in MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3F, G, H).

claim: Unlike WT CHIKV, CHIKV E2 K200R particles remained stably detectable in the serum for at least 1 hr post-inoculation.
source: Indeed, unlike WT CHIKV, which is efficiently cleared from the circulation, CHIKV E2 K200R particles remained stably detectable in the serum for at least 1 hr post-inoculation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Differential clearance of WT and E2 K200R CHIKV particles was maintained when virions were derived from human fibroblasts.
source: Importantly, the differential clearance was not dependent on the cell type from which the viral particles were derived, as differential clearance of WT and E2 K200R CHIKV particles was maintained when virions were derived from human fibroblasts, a clinically relevant cell type (Couderc et al., 2008) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The E2 K200R mutation did not impact the stability of viral particles in serum.
source: The E2 K200R mutation did not impact the stability of viral particles in serum, demonstrating that this effect was not due to differential stability of WT and E2 K200R CHIKV particles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The levels of E2 K200R CHIKV particles in control PLL-treated mice were indistinguishable from WT and E2 K200R CHIKV particles in the circulation of mice pre-treated with CLL.
source: Moreover, the levels of E2 K200R CHIKV particles in control PLL-treated mice were indistinguishable from WT and E2 K200R CHIKV particles in the circulation of mice pre-treated with CLL (Figure 4C), demonstrating that CHIKV E2 K200R allows for evasion of phagocytic cell-mediated clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CHIKV E2 K200R allows for evasion of phagocytic cell-mediated clearance.
source: Moreover, the levels of E2 K200R CHIKV particles in control PLL-treated mice were indistinguishable from WT and E2 K200R CHIKV particles in the circulation of mice pre-treated with CLL (Figure 4C), demonstrating that CHIKV E2 K200R allows for evasion of phagocytic cell-mediated clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Evasion of clearance by E2 K200R was observed in C57BL/6J, 129S1/SvImJ, and BALB/cJ mouse strains.
source: The ability of E2 K200R to evade this response was not limited to WT C57BL/6J mice (Figure 4C), as evasion of clearance also was observed in 129S1/SvImJ, and BALB/cJ mouse strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: All WT strains of CHIKV and ONNV were cleared from the circulation at 45 min post-inoculation.
source: Similar to CHIKV AF15561, all WT strains of CHIKV and ONNV were cleared from the circulation at 45 min post-inoculation, whereas the levels of all E2 K200R mutant particles were substantially higher (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The levels of all E2 K200R mutant CHIKV and ONNV particles were substantially higher in circulation at 45 min post-inoculation compared to WT strains.
source: Similar to CHIKV AF15561, all WT strains of CHIKV and ONNV were cleared from the circulation at 45 min post-inoculation, whereas the levels of all E2 K200R mutant particles were substantially higher (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: An E2 K200R mutation broadly facilitates evasion of phagocytic-cell mediated clearance in multiple CHIKV strains and ONNV.
source: These results demonstrate that an E2 K200R mutation broadly facilitates evasion of phagocytic-cell mediated clearance in multiple CHIKV strains, as well as the related ONNV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing E2 K200R mutation effects across multiple CHIKV strains and ONNV (Figure 4D).

claim: Viral burdens in the serum were significantly higher in mice inoculated with E2 K200R strains at 1 d post-inoculation following subcutaneous inoculation.
source: Viral burdens in the serum were significantly higher in mice inoculated with E2 K200R strains (Figure 5A), indicating that phagocytic cell-mediated clearance is an important immune mechanism to control viremia following subcutaneous inoculation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Phagocytic cell-mediated clearance is an important immune mechanism to control viremia following subcutaneous inoculation.
source: Viral burdens in the serum were significantly higher in mice inoculated with E2 K200R strains (Figure 5A), indicating that phagocytic cell-mediated clearance is an important immune mechanism to control viremia following subcutaneous inoculation.
evidence: Inferred from higher viremia in mice infected with E2 K200R strains (Figure 5A).

claim: Significantly elevated levels of virus were detected in the contralateral right ankle of mice infected with E2 K200R strains at 1 d post-inoculation.
source: Moreover, although viral burdens were similar in tissues proximal to the site of inoculation (i.e, the L. ankle), significantly elevated levels of virus were detected in the contralateral right ankle of mice infected with E2 K200R strains (Figure 5A), demonstrating that this mutation facilitates more rapid viral dissemination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The E2 K200R mutation facilitates more rapid viral dissemination.
source: Moreover, although viral burdens were similar in tissues proximal to the site of inoculation (i.e, the L. ankle), significantly elevated levels of virus were detected in the contralateral right ankle of mice infected with E2 K200R strains (Figure 5A), demonstrating that this mutation facilitates more rapid viral dissemination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing elevated virus in distal tissues (Figure 5A).

claim: Infection of MARCO-/- mice with WT CHIKV resulted in an elevated viremia at 1 d post-inoculation compared with infection of WT mice.
source: Similar to infection of WT mice with CHIKV E2 K200R, infection of MARCO-/- mice with WT CHIKV resulted in an elevated viremia and more rapid viral dissemination to distal sites including the right ankle and quadriceps compared with infection of WT mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Infection of MARCO-/- mice with WT CHIKV resulted in more rapid viral dissemination to distal sites including the right ankle and quadriceps compared with infection of WT mice.
source: Similar to infection of WT mice with CHIKV E2 K200R, infection of MARCO-/- mice with WT CHIKV resulted in an elevated viremia and more rapid viral dissemination to distal sites including the right ankle and quadriceps compared with infection of WT mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MARCO-dependent clearance of circulating CHIKV particles controls viremia and impedes viral dissemination.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that MARCO-dependent clearance of circulating CHIKV particles controls viremia and impedes viral dissemination.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing elevated viremia and dissemination in MARCO-/- mice (Figure 5B).

claim: Similar levels of WT CHIKV and E2 K200R were detected in the bodies, legs and saliva of infected mosquitoes at 3 d post-infection.
source: Following blood-feeding inoculation of mosquitoes, similar levels of WT CHIKV and E2 K200R were detected in the bodies, legs and saliva of infected mosquitoes at 3 d post-infection, suggesting that in contrast to mice, the E2 K200R mutation had no impact on viral dissemination in mosquitoes (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The E2 K200R mutation had no impact on viral dissemination in mosquitoes.
source: Following blood-feeding inoculation of mosquitoes, similar levels of WT CHIKV and E2 K200R were detected in the bodies, legs and saliva of infected mosquitoes at 3 d post-infection, suggesting that in contrast to mice, the E2 K200R mutation had no impact on viral dissemination in mosquitoes (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from similar viral levels in mosquito tissues (Figure 6A).

claim: The CHIKV-ApaI genetic marker does not influence viral fitness in C6/36 cells.
source: Control 1:1 competitions of CHIKV and CHIKV-ApaI in C6/36 cells (Figure 6B) and microinjected Ae. Aegypti mosquitoes (Figure 6C and D) demonstrated that the genetic marker does not influence viral fitness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The CHIKV-ApaI genetic marker does not influence viral fitness in microinjected Ae. aegypti mosquitoes.
source: Control 1:1 competitions of CHIKV and CHIKV-ApaI in C6/36 cells (Figure 6B) and microinjected Ae. Aegypti mosquitoes (Figure 6C and D) demonstrated that the genetic marker does not influence viral fitness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Direct 1:1 competition of CHIKV and CHIKV E2 K200R showed no selective disadvantage to WT virus in the mosquito vector.
source: Similar results were observed following direct 1:1 competition of CHIKV and CHIKV E2 K200R, (Figure 6B, C and D), suggesting that the E2 K200R mutation has no selective disadvantage to WT virus in the mosquito vector.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C and D.

claim: The E2 K200R mutation has no selective disadvantage to WT virus in the mosquito vector.
source: Similar results were observed following direct 1:1 competition of CHIKV and CHIKV E2 K200R, (Figure 6B, C and D), suggesting that the E2 K200R mutation has no selective disadvantage to WT virus in the mosquito vector.
evidence: Inferred from competition experiments showing no fitness difference (Figure 6B, C and D).

claim: While the E2 K200R mutation dramatically influences CHIKV dissemination in the vertebrate host, it is neutral in the mosquito vector.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that while the E2 K200R mutation dramatically influences CHIKV dissemination in the vertebrate host, it is neutral in the mosquito vector.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing effects in mice but not mosquitoes (Figures 5, 6).

claim: RRV strain DC5692 was efficiently cleared from the circulation by phagocytic cells.
source: In addition to RRV strain SN11 (Figure 1C), a 2009 clinical isolate (Liu et al., 2011), we found that RRV strain DC5692 (Jupille et al., 2011; Lindsay, 1996) also was efficiently cleared from the circulation by phagocytic cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: RRV strain T48 was resistant to clearance from the circulation.
source: In contrast, RRV strain T48 (Doherty and Whitehead, 1963) was resistant to clearance, and clearance was relatively unaffected by prior depletion of phagocytic cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Clearance of RRV strain T48 was relatively unaffected by prior depletion of phagocytic cells.
source: In contrast, RRV strain T48 (Doherty and Whitehead, 1963) was resistant to clearance, and clearance was relatively unaffected by prior depletion of phagocytic cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The genetic determinant of RRV susceptibility to clearance was mapped to a region of the genome encoding a portion of capsid, E3 and E2.
source: Through chimeric virus analysis of DC5692 and T48 strains, we mapped the genetic determinant of RRV susceptibility to clearance to a region of the genome encoding a portion of capsid, E3 and E2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutating position E2 251 of RRV T48 from arginine to lysine (R251K) was sufficient to make this strain more susceptible to clearance.
source: Remarkably, mutating position E2 251 of T48 from arginine to lysine (R251K) was sufficient to make this strain more susceptible to clearance, while the corresponding K251R mutation in DC5692 conferred resistance to clearance (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The K251R mutation in RRV DC5692 conferred resistance to clearance.
source: Remarkably, mutating position E2 251 of T48 from arginine to lysine (R251K) was sufficient to make this strain more susceptible to clearance, while the corresponding K251R mutation in DC5692 conferred resistance to clearance (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: RRV strain SN11 has a lysine at E2 251.
source: Moreover, sequencing analysis confirmed the presence of a lysine at E2 251 in RRV strain SN11.
evidence: Supported by sequencing analysis.

claim: The R251K mutation had no impact on the stability of RRV T48 in serum.
source: The R251K mutation had no impact on the stability of RRV T48 in serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inoculation of purified viral particles generated in serum free media maintained the differential clearance of T48 and T48 E2 R251K.
source: In addition, inoculation of purified viral particles generated in serum free media maintained the differential clearance of T48 and T48 E2 R251K, indicating that viral clearance is not mediated by factors in fetal bovine serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Viral clearance is not mediated by factors in fetal bovine serum.
source: In addition, inoculation of purified viral particles generated in serum free media maintained the differential clearance of T48 and T48 E2 R251K, indicating that viral clearance is not mediated by factors in fetal bovine serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from maintained differential clearance with serum-free purified particles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).

claim: In three independent alphaviruses, lysine to arginine mutations at distinct sites in the E2 glycoprotein allow for viral escape from phagocytic cell-mediated clearance.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that, in three independent alphaviruses, lysine to arginine mutations at distinct sites in the E2 glycoprotein (Figure 7C) allow for viral escape from phagocytic cell-mediated clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data across CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV (Figures 4, 7).

claim: All substitutions away from lysine at CHIKV E2 200 prevented efficient clearance of circulating CHIKV particles.
source: Remarkably, all substitutions tested prevented efficient clearance of circulating CHIKV particles following i.v. inoculation (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: All substitutions away from lysine at RRV E2 251 allowed for RRV escape from phagocytic cell-mediated clearance.
source: Moreover, a subset of these mutations was introduced at position E2 251 of RRV, and again all substitutions away from lysine allowed for RRV escape from phagocytic cell-mediated clearance (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Clearance of alphavirus particles from the circulation is strictly dependent on the presence of a lysine residue at E2 200 (CHIKV) or E2 251 (RRV).
source: These findings suggest that clearance of these alphavirus particles from the circulation is strictly dependent on the presence of a lysine residue at E2 200 (CHIKV) or E2 251 (RRV).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing all non-lysine substitutions allow clearance evasion (Figure 8B, C).

claim: The critical lysine residue that mediates clearance in RRV (E2 K251) is conserved in CHIKV (E2 K252).
source: The critical lysine residue that mediates clearance in RRV (E2 K251) is conserved in CHIKV (E2 K252).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison and structural knowledge.

claim: CHIKV E2 K252R remained susceptible to clearance by phagocytic cells.
source: However, we found that CHIKV E2 K252R remained susceptible to clearance by phagocytic cells (Figure 8D), suggesting that, in contrast to RRV, a lysine at this position in E2 is not required for CHIKV clearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A lysine at E2 252 in CHIKV is not required for CHIKV clearance.
source: However, we found that CHIKV E2 K252R remained susceptible to clearance by phagocytic cells (Figure 8D), suggesting that, in contrast to RRV, a lysine at this position in E2 is not required for CHIKV clearance.
evidence: Inferred from maintained clearance of CHIKV E2 K252R (Figure 8D).

claim: Specific lysine residues in the E2 glycoproteins of CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV facilitate phagocytic cell-mediated clearance of viral particles from the circulation of a vertebrate host.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate that specific lysine residues in the E2 glycoproteins of CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV facilitate phagocytic cell-mediated clearance of viral particles from the circulation of a vertebrate host.
evidence: Supported by experimental data across multiple alphaviruses (Figures 4, 7, 8).

claim: Liver KCs have been implicated as a critical innate defense against blood-borne bacterial pathogens.
source: While liver KCs have been implicated as a critical innate defense against blood-borne bacterial pathogens (Jenne and Kubes, 2013; Krenkel and Tacke, 2017; Kubes and Jenne, 2018), this work expands their role to additionally serve as sentinels for circulating CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jenne and Kubes, 2013; Krenkel and Tacke, 2017; Kubes and Jenne, 2018.

claim: This work expands the role of liver KCs to additionally serve as sentinels for circulating CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV.
source: While liver KCs have been implicated as a critical innate defense against blood-borne bacterial pathogens (Jenne and Kubes, 2013; Krenkel and Tacke, 2017; Kubes and Jenne, 2018), this work expands their role to additionally serve as sentinels for circulating CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing KC-mediated clearance of alphaviruses (Figure 2).

claim: The innate clearance pathway for alphaviruses occurs independently of opsonization with natural antibody or fragments of C3.
source: Mechanistically, this innate clearance pathway occurs independently of opsonization with natural antibody or fragments of C3, and instead is mediated by the scavenger receptor MARCO.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in μMT and C3-/- mice (Figure 3A, B).

claim: The innate clearance pathway for alphaviruses is mediated by the scavenger receptor MARCO.
source: Mechanistically, this innate clearance pathway occurs independently of opsonization with natural antibody or fragments of C3, and instead is mediated by the scavenger receptor MARCO.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in MARCO-/- mice (Figure 3F, G, H).

claim: MARCO is known to be expressed by marginal zone macrophages (MZM) in the spleen.
source: While our data suggest that KCs in the liver are primarily responsible for clearance of these alphavirus particles from the circulation, MARCO is known to be expressed by other macrophage populations exposed to the blood, including MZM in the spleen (Borges da Silva et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Borges da Silva et al., 2015.

claim: Following serial passage in cell culture, alphaviruses frequently acquire adaptive mutations that enhance interactions between viral particles and GAGs.
source: Following serial passage in cell culture, alphaviruses frequently acquire adaptive mutations that enhance interactions between viral particles and GAGs. (Bernard et al., 2000; Byrnes and Griffin, 1998; Heil et al., 2001; Klimstra et al., 1998; Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2000; Byrnes and Griffin, 1998; Heil et al., 2001; Klimstra et al., 1998; Silva et al., 2014.

claim: Alphaviruses that have acquired enhanced in vitro GAG binding are rapidly cleared from the circulation of mice.
source: Alphaviruses that have acquired enhanced in vitro GAG binding are rapidly cleared from the circulation of mice (Bernard et al., 2000; Byrnes and Griffin, 2000), suggesting that virion-GAG interactions are one mechanism that can determine the magnitude and duration of arboviral viremia.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bernard et al., 2000; Byrnes and Griffin, 2000.

claim: Opsonization of DENV particles by mannose binding lectin (MBL) accelerated their clearance from the circulation of mice.
source: Beyond GAGs, previous work demonstrated that opsonization of DENV particles by mannose binding lectin (MBL), which can neutralize particles via a C3-dependent mechanism, accelerated their clearance from the circulation of mice (Fuchs et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2010.

claim: The clearance of circulating CHIKV and RRV particles was inhibited by pre-treatment of mice with the SR competitive inhibitors poly(I) and dextran sulfate.
source: We found that the clearance of circulating CHIKV and RRV particles was inhibited by pre-treatment of mice with the SR competitive inhibitors poly(I) and dextran sulfate (Platt and Gordon, 1998), supporting a role for SRs in clearance of these alphaviruses from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: Poly(I) and dextran sulfate are known ligands for the class A scavenger receptors SR-A1 and MARCO.
source: Poly(I) and dextran sulfate are known ligands for the class A scavenger receptors SR-A1 and MARCO (Chen et al., 2006; Platt and Gordon, 1998), both of which are transcriptionally expressed in liver KCs (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2006; Platt and Gordon, 1998.

claim: SR-A1 and MARCO are transcriptionally expressed in liver KCs.
source: Poly(I) and dextran sulfate are known ligands for the class A scavenger receptors SR-A1 and MARCO (Chen et al., 2006; Platt and Gordon, 1998), both of which are transcriptionally expressed in liver KCs (Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tabula Muris Consortium et al., 2018.

claim: SR-A1 has a protective role during systemic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection of mice.
source: SR-A1 has a protective role during systemic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection of mice (Suzuki et al., 1997), and HSV-1 can utilize MARCO for attachment and entry into epithelial cells (MacLeod et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suzuki et al., 1997.

claim: HSV-1 can utilize MARCO for attachment and entry into epithelial cells.
source: SR-A1 has a protective role during systemic herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection of mice (Suzuki et al., 1997), and HSV-1 can utilize MARCO for attachment and entry into epithelial cells (MacLeod et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to MacLeod et al., 2013.

claim: Vaccinia virus (VacV) binding to MARCO on keratinocytes enhances infection of these cells in vitro.
source: Similarly, vaccinia virus (VacV) binding to MARCO on keratinocytes enhances infection of these cells in vitro (MacLeod et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to MacLeod et al., 2015.

claim: MARCO mediates transduction of macrophages by adenovirus in vitro.
source: MARCO also mediates transduction of macrophages by adenovirus in vitro, and appears to promote innate immune responses to the infection (Maler et al., 2017), suggesting that MARCO-virus interactions can regulate host cell responses to infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maler et al., 2017.

claim: MARCO appears to promote innate immune responses to adenovirus infection.
source: MARCO also mediates transduction of macrophages by adenovirus in vitro, and appears to promote innate immune responses to the infection (Maler et al., 2017), suggesting that MARCO-virus interactions can regulate host cell responses to infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maler et al., 2017.

claim: MARCO-virus interactions can regulate host cell responses to infection.
source: MARCO also mediates transduction of macrophages by adenovirus in vitro, and appears to promote innate immune responses to the infection (Maler et al., 2017), suggesting that MARCO-virus interactions can regulate host cell responses to infection.
evidence: Inferred from MARCO's role in promoting innate immune responses to adenovirus (Maler et al., 2017).

claim: N-linked glycosylation of DENV and WNV glycoproteins was previously found to influence clearance of these viral particles from the circulation of mice.
source: N-linked glycosylation of DENV and WNV glycoproteins was previously found to influence clearance of these viral particles from the circulation of mice (Fuchs et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2010.

claim: Mutation of the predicted surface-exposed CHIKV E2 glycosylation sites had no impact on the clearance of CHIKV particles from the circulation.
source: However, we found that mutation of the predicted surface-exposed CHIKV E2 glycosylation sites had no impact on the clearance of CHIKV particles from the circulation, suggesting that clearance occurs independent of E2 glycosylation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CHIKV E2 K200R was isolated from the serum of a Rag1-/- mouse chronically infected with an Asian genotype CHIKV strain.
source: CHIKV E2 K200R was isolated from the serum of a Rag1-/- mouse chronically infected with an Asian genotype CHIKV strain (Hawman et al., 2017), suggesting that this mutation arose as a mechanism to evade phagocytic cell-mediated clearance from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hawman et al., 2017.

claim: The CHIKV E2 K200R mutation arose as a mechanism to evade phagocytic cell-mediated clearance from the circulation.
source: CHIKV E2 K200R was isolated from the serum of a Rag1-/- mouse chronically infected with an Asian genotype CHIKV strain (Hawman et al., 2017), suggesting that this mutation arose as a mechanism to evade phagocytic cell-mediated clearance from the circulation.
evidence: Inferred from isolation of E2 K200R from chronically infected mouse and its clearance evasion phenotype.

claim: E2 K200 is conserved in the closely related alphavirus ONNV.
source: Moreover, E2 K200 is conserved in the closely related alphavirus ONNV, and introduction of an E2 K200R mutation in this independent alphavirus species also allowed for escape from clearance from the circulation.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison.

claim: Introduction of an E2 K200R mutation in ONNV allowed for escape from clearance from the circulation.
source: Moreover, E2 K200 is conserved in the closely related alphavirus ONNV, and introduction of an E2 K200R mutation in this independent alphavirus species also allowed for escape from clearance from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: RRV has an asparagine at E2 200.
source: While we found that circulating RRV particles also are susceptible to clearance by phagocytic cells, RRV has an asparagine at E2 200, suggesting that a viral feature other than E2 K200 promotes the clearance of circulating RRV particles.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison.

claim: A viral feature other than E2 K200 promotes the clearance of circulating RRV particles.
source: While we found that circulating RRV particles also are susceptible to clearance by phagocytic cells, RRV has an asparagine at E2 200, suggesting that a viral feature other than E2 K200 promotes the clearance of circulating RRV particles.
evidence: Inferred from RRV clearance despite lacking lysine at E2 200.

claim: A lysine residue at RRV E2 251 is essential for efficient clearance of RRV particles from the circulation.
source: Through chimeric and mutational analysis of susceptible (DC5692) and resistant (T48) RRV strains, we discovered that a lysine residue at E2 251 is essential for efficient clearance of RRV particles from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Discrete lysine residues in the E2 glycoprotein of three independent alphaviruses promote their efficient clearance from the circulation.
source: Thus, discrete lysine residues in the E2 glycoprotein of three independent alphaviruses promote their efficient clearance from the circulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data across CHIKV, ONNV, and RRV (Figures 4, 7, 8).

claim: Lysine is frequently post-translationally modified.
source: A number of observations from this study and previously published studies support this idea, including (1) an E2 K200R mutation functions in a variety of distinct genetic backgrounds to facilitate escape of circulating CHIKV and ONNV particles from MARCO-dependent clearance; (2) a lysine residue at a distinct site in RRV E2 is essential for phagocytic-cell mediated clearance of circulating RRV particles; (3) while the lysine that mediates RRV clearance is conserved in CHIKV, mutating this lysine has no impact on clearance of circulating CHIKV particles; (4) lysine is frequently post-translationally modified, and can be modified with a diverse range of post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Azevedo and Saiardi, 2016); and (5) SRs were initially identified based on their capacity to capture lysine acetylated low density lipoprotein (Platt and Gordon, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Azevedo and Saiardi, 2016.

claim: Lysine can be modified with a diverse range of post-translational modifications (PTMs).
source: A number of observations from this study and previously published studies support this idea, including (1) an E2 K200R mutation functions in a variety of distinct genetic backgrounds to facilitate escape of circulating CHIKV and ONNV particles from MARCO-dependent clearance; (2) a lysine residue at a distinct site in RRV E2 is essential for phagocytic-cell mediated clearance of circulating RRV particles; (3) while the lysine that mediates RRV clearance is conserved in CHIKV, mutating this lysine has no impact on clearance of circulating CHIKV particles; (4) lysine is frequently post-translationally modified, and can be modified with a diverse range of post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Azevedo and Saiardi, 2016); and (5) SRs were initially identified based on their capacity to capture lysine acetylated low density lipoprotein (Platt and Gordon, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Azevedo and Saiardi, 2016.

claim: SRs were initially identified based on their capacity to capture lysine acetylated low density lipoprotein.
source: A number of observations from this study and previously published studies support this idea, including (1) an E2 K200R mutation functions in a variety of distinct genetic backgrounds to facilitate escape of circulating CHIKV and ONNV particles from MARCO-dependent clearance; (2) a lysine residue at a distinct site in RRV E2 is essential for phagocytic-cell mediated clearance of circulating RRV particles; (3) while the lysine that mediates RRV clearance is conserved in CHIKV, mutating this lysine has no impact on clearance of circulating CHIKV particles; (4) lysine is frequently post-translationally modified, and can be modified with a diverse range of post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Azevedo and Saiardi, 2016); and (5) SRs were initially identified based on their capacity to capture lysine acetylated low density lipoprotein (Platt and Gordon, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Platt and Gordon, 1998.

claim: 1,333 out of 1,335 CHIKV sequences in the ViPR database encode a lysine at position E2 200.
source: Analysis of E2 protein sequences in the ViPR database (Pickett et al., 2012) revealed that 1,333/1,335 CHIKV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 200 (2/1,335 encode an arginine), 8/8 ONNV sequences encode a lysine, and 187/204 available RRV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 251, while the remaining 17 encode an arginine.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ViPR database sequences.

claim: 2 out of 1,335 CHIKV sequences in the ViPR database encode an arginine at position E2 200.
source: Analysis of E2 protein sequences in the ViPR database (Pickett et al., 2012) revealed that 1,333/1,335 CHIKV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 200 (2/1,335 encode an arginine), 8/8 ONNV sequences encode a lysine, and 187/204 available RRV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 251, while the remaining 17 encode an arginine.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ViPR database sequences.

claim: 8 out of 8 ONNV sequences in the ViPR database encode a lysine at position E2 200.
source: Analysis of E2 protein sequences in the ViPR database (Pickett et al., 2012) revealed that 1,333/1,335 CHIKV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 200 (2/1,335 encode an arginine), 8/8 ONNV sequences encode a lysine, and 187/204 available RRV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 251, while the remaining 17 encode an arginine.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ViPR database sequences.

claim: 187 out of 204 available RRV sequences in the ViPR database encode a lysine at position E2 251.
source: Analysis of E2 protein sequences in the ViPR database (Pickett et al., 2012) revealed that 1,333/1,335 CHIKV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 200 (2/1,335 encode an arginine), 8/8 ONNV sequences encode a lysine, and 187/204 available RRV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 251, while the remaining 17 encode an arginine.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ViPR database sequences.

claim: 17 out of 204 available RRV sequences in the ViPR database encode an arginine at position E2 251.
source: Analysis of E2 protein sequences in the ViPR database (Pickett et al., 2012) revealed that 1,333/1,335 CHIKV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 200 (2/1,335 encode an arginine), 8/8 ONNV sequences encode a lysine, and 187/204 available RRV sequences encode a lysine at position E2 251, while the remaining 17 encode an arginine.
evidence: Supported by analysis of ViPR database sequences.

claim: Genes encoding SRs, including MARCO, exhibit substantial genetic variation in both humans and mice.
source: Alternatively, the susceptibility or resistance of circulating alphavirus particles to clearance may be influenced by polymorphisms in SRs. Genes encoding SRs, including MARCO, exhibit substantial genetic variation in both humans and mice (Bowdish and Gordon, 2009) and this variation can have functional consequences.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bowdish and Gordon, 2009.

claim: Genetic variation in SRs can have functional consequences.
source: Alternatively, the susceptibility or resistance of circulating alphavirus particles to clearance may be influenced by polymorphisms in SRs. Genes encoding SRs, including MARCO, exhibit substantial genetic variation in both humans and mice (Bowdish and Gordon, 2009) and this variation can have functional consequences.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bowdish and Gordon, 2009.

claim: Position 252 of MARCO is known to be polymorphic in humans.
source: For example, position 252 of MARCO is known to be polymorphic in humans, and the less common variant has a decreased capacity to phagocytize bacteria in vitro (Novakowski et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Novakowski et al., 2018.

claim: The less common variant of MARCO at position 252 has a decreased capacity to phagocytize bacteria in vitro.
source: For example, position 252 of MARCO is known to be polymorphic in humans, and the less common variant has a decreased capacity to phagocytize bacteria in vitro (Novakowski et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Novakowski et al., 2018.

claim: SNPs within human SRs associate with differential susceptibility to various pathogens.
source: Consistent with this, SNPs within human SRs associate with differential susceptibility to various pathogens (Bowdish et al., 2013; High et al., 2016; Lao et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2011; Westhaus et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bowdish et al., 2013; High et al., 2016; Lao et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2011; Westhaus et al., 2017.

claim: Human patients exhibit a high degree of variability in peak viremia and disease severity following alphavirus infections.
source: Following alphavirus infections, human patients exhibit a high degree of variability in peak viremia and disease severity (Chow et al., 2011; de St Maurice et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2017; Thiberville et al., 2013; Vaughn et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chow et al., 2011; de St Maurice et al., 2018; Musso et al., 2017; Thiberville et al., 2013; Vaughn et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 2016.

claim: Inter- or intra-host variability within SRs may influence the susceptibility of alphaviruses to SR-dependent clearance from the circulation.
source: Given this, inter- or intra-host variability within SRs may influence the susceptibility of alphaviruses to SR-dependent clearance from the circulation, contributing to variability in viremia and disease outcomes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on known SR polymorphisms and their functional effects.

claim: MARCO is evolving under positive selection.
source: Furthermore, MARCO is evolving under positive selection (Yap et al., 2015), a signature often associated with host-viral conflicts.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yap et al., 2015.

claim: Positive selection is a signature often associated with host-viral conflicts.
source: Furthermore, MARCO is evolving under positive selection (Yap et al., 2015), a signature often associated with host-viral conflicts.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about evolutionary signatures.

claim: The CHIKV E2 K200R strain that escapes MARCO-dependent clearance generates a higher viremia, disseminates to distal sites more rapidly, and causes more severe disease outcomes in mice.
source: The CHIKV E2 K200R strain that escapes MARCO-dependent clearance generates a higher viremia, disseminates to distal sites more rapidly, and causes more severe disease outcomes in mice (Hawman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hawman et al., 2017.

claim: Depletion of phagocytic cells with clodronate liposomes resulted in a higher magnitude and duration of viremia following subcutaneous CHIKV infection of mice.
source: Consistent with our data, prior studies found that some strains of Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus accumulated in the liver following i.v. inoculation of hamsters (Jahrling and Gorelkin, 1975) and that depletion of phagocytic cells with clodronate liposomes resulted in a higher magnitude and duration of viremia following subcutaneous CHIKV infection of mice (Gardner et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gardner et al., 2010.

claim: Clodronate liposome depletion of phagocytic cells enhanced WNV viremia and disease severity in mice.
source: Similarly, clodronate liposome depletion of phagocytic cells enhanced WNV viremia and disease severity in mice (Bryan et al., 2018), suggesting that phagocytic cell-mediated clearance of circulating arboviruses has implications that span virus genera.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bryan et al., 2018.

claim: Phagocytic cell-mediated clearance of circulating arboviruses has implications that span virus genera.
source: Similarly, clodronate liposome depletion of phagocytic cells enhanced WNV viremia and disease severity in mice (Bryan et al., 2018), suggesting that phagocytic cell-mediated clearance of circulating arboviruses has implications that span virus genera.
evidence: Inferred from similar effects observed with WNV (Bryan et al., 2018) and alphaviruses.

claim: WNV and Japanese Encephalitis virus are unable to generate a viremia of sufficient magnitude in humans to infect a mosquito vector and propagate the transmission cycle.
source: While some arboviruses, such as WNV and Japanese Encephalitis virus, are unable to generate a viremia of sufficient magnitude in humans to infect a mosquito vector and propagate the transmission cycle (Weaver, 2018), others like CHIKV, DENV, and Zika virus are readily amplified through human-mosquito-human cycles (Weaver, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weaver, 2018.

claim: CHIKV, DENV, and Zika virus are readily amplified through human-mosquito-human cycles.
source: While some arboviruses, such as WNV and Japanese Encephalitis virus, are unable to generate a viremia of sufficient magnitude in humans to infect a mosquito vector and propagate the transmission cycle (Weaver, 2018), others like CHIKV, DENV, and Zika virus are readily amplified through human-mosquito-human cycles (Weaver, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weaver, 2018.

claim: Susceptibility or resistance to clearance by liver macrophages and SRs may contribute to whether humans are dead-end hosts for an arbovirus or can fuel widespread epidemics.
source: Susceptibility or resistance to clearance by liver macrophages, other scavenging cell types such as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, and SRs may contribute to whether humans are dead-end hosts for an arbovirus or can fuel widespread epidemics.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the role of clearance mechanisms in controlling viremia.
